q.t: How many letters does the musical alphabet use?
q.e: A B C D E F G — then it starts again at A.

q.t: Which letter comes after G?
q.e: The letters go round in a circle: after G comes A again, one octave higher. (G♯ sits between G and A, but the next letter is A.)

q.t: What does a sharp (♯) do to a note?
o: Raises it by a half step
Lowers it by a half step
q.e: Sharp = one half step up.

q.t: What does a flat (♭) do to a note?
o: Lowers it by a half step
Raises it by a half step
q.e: Flat = one half step down.

q.t: How many different notes are there in one octave?
q.e: 7 letters plus 5 sharps/flats in between = 12 notes.

q.t: On a guitar, a half step is…
q.e: Each fret raises the note by one half step.

q.t: On a guitar, a whole step is…
q.e: A whole step = two half steps = two frets.

q.t: Which pair has no note in between?
q.e: B–C and E–F are already a half step apart, so nothing fits in between.

q.t: What is the note just above C?
q.e: One half step above C is C♯ (also called D♭).

q.t: C♯ and D♭ are…
o: the same note with two names
q.e: One half step above C and one half step below D land on the same note.

q.t: Which pair has no note in between?
q.e: B–C and E–F are the two natural half steps.

q.t: What is another name for G♯?
q.e: G♯ is one step above G and one step below A, so it is also A♭.

q.t: What is another name for E♭?
q.e: One step below E is the same note as one step above D: D♯ = E♭.

q.t: What is one half step above E?
q.e: E to F is already a half step, so the next note above E is F.

q.t: What is one half step above B?
q.e: B to C is already a half step, so the next note above B is C.

q.t: What is one whole step above C?
q.e: C → C♯ (1) → D (2). Two half steps = one whole step.

q.t: What is one whole step above E?
q.e: E → F (1) → F♯ (2). Careful: E to F is only a half step.

q.t: Going down, we usually name the in-between notes as…
q.e: Going down: E, E♭, D, D♭, C … Going up we use sharps.

q.t: On a piano, the black keys are the…
q.e: White keys are the 7 letters; black keys are the 5 sharps/flats in between.

q.t: How many sharps/flats are there in one octave?
q.e: 12 notes − 7 letters = 5 in-between notes.

q.t: What is 3 half steps above G?
What is 2 half steps above B?
q.e: B → C (1) → C♯ (2). B to C is only one half step.

q.t: What is 4 half steps above C?
What is 2 half steps below C?
q.e: Going down: C → B (1) → B♭ (2). B♭ is the same note as A♯.

q.t: How many half steps from E up to A?
How many half steps from A up to C?
How many half steps from C up to the next C?
q.e: One octave = all 12 notes.

q.t: Why is there no note between E and F?
o: E–F was already a small gap when the letters were named
Nobody has found a note there yet
F is too high to have a sharp
q.e: The 7 letters came from an old scale where B–C and E–F were already half steps. The extra notes only fitted into the big gaps.

q.t: Which of these is not a new note of its own?
q.e: E♯ is just F, because E to F is already a half step.

q.t: Each half step makes the note shake about how many times faster?
q.e: 12 half steps double the frequency, so each one is a small step of about × 1.06.

q.t: What is 7 half steps above C?
q.e: C, C♯, D, D♯, E, F, F♯, G — the 7th step is G.

q.t: What is 5 half steps above B?
What is 3 half steps below F?
q.e: Going down: F → E (1) → E♭ (2) → D (3).

q.t: How many half steps from F up to the next C?
q.e: F → F♯ → G → G♯ → A → A♯ → B → C: 7 steps.

q.t: How many half steps from G up to the next D?
q.e: G → G♯ → A → A♯ → B → C → C♯ → D: 7 steps.

q.t: How many whole steps make one octave?
q.e: 12 half steps ÷ 2 = 6 whole steps.

q.t: Which group are all the same note?
q.e: B♯ = one half step above B = C. (F♭ is E, not F; A♯ and A♭ are on opposite sides of A.)

q.t: Seven half steps up makes the shakes about × 1.5. Why do these two notes blend so well?
o: 3 shakes match 2 shakes, so they line up often
They are both on open strings
q.e: A simple ratio (3:2) means the shakes of the two notes keep lining up, which our ears hear as smooth. It is the sound of a power chord.

q.t: A note is called A♯ going up. What would you call it going down?
q.e: The note between A and B is A♯ going up and B♭ going down.

q.t: Starting on E, which list climbs by half steps correctly?
q.e: E → F is a half step (no E♯ in between), then F♯, then G.
